claims.sentence: No king is named.
claims.claim: Psalm 76 names no king.

claims.sentence: No enemy dead are counted.
claims.claim: Psalm 76 gives no count of enemy dead.

claims.sentence: The stranger absence is this: no one in the poem ever says "we."
claims.claim: Psalm 76 contains no first-person-plural speaker saying “we.”

claims.sentence: There is no "us," no "our," no "I."
claims.claim: Psalm 76 contains none of those first-person references to its speakers.

claims.sentence: Psalm 46 has a refrain: ה׳ צְבָקוֹת עִמָּנוּ מִשְׂגָּב־לָנוּ אֱלֹקֵי יַעֲקֹב, "YHWH of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our stronghold" (46:8, 12).

claims.sentence: Psalm 76 uses the same title, אֱלֹקֵי יַעֲקֹב, "God of Jacob" (v. 7), and attaches it to no one.
claims.claim: Psalm 76:7 uses “God of Jacob” without Psalm 46’s “with us” or “our” language.

claims.sentence: He is known in Judah, housed in Salem and Zion, and "there" He breaks arrows, shield, sword, and finally war itself.
claims.claim: Psalm 76:2–4 locates God in Judah, Salem, and Zion and lists bow-arrows, shield, sword, and war among what He breaks there.

claims.sentence: (Selah is a musical or liturgical marker whose exact sense is lost; it seems to signal a pause.)

claims.sentence: The one verb of resistance, "stand," appears only inside a question that expects no answer: וּמִי־יַעֲמֹד לְפָנֶיךָ, "who can stand before You?" (v. 8).

claims.sentence: The verb is the same, and so is the climb from weapon to abstraction.
claims.claim: Psalm 76:4 and Hosea 2:20 use forms of the same verb, שבר, in lists proceeding from weapons to war.

claims.sentence: In Hosea it is Israel who lies down, safe at last.
claims.claim: In Hosea 2:20, the beneficiaries of safety, rather than the attackers, are made to lie down.

claims.sentence: Their slumber in v. 6 deepens in v. 7 into the heavy, God-sent unconsciousness the Bible calls תַּרְדֵּמָה, *tardemah*.

claims.sentence: Beside the lair stands the city's archaic name, Salem, which sounds like "peace."
